title: Why Playing Favorites Is Bad For Classroom Management nagement/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin confronts teacher favoritism, describing the small daily differences in warmth, attention, and patience shown toward "likeable" students versus those seen as difficult. He argues favoritism is usually invisible to the teacher, hidden behind self-justifications, even though it is plainly obvious to students. He details its costs: it creates a social class system in the room, breeds resentment, weakens self-confidence in less-favored students, further alienates already-struggling students, produces an unhappy classroom, and undermines a teacher's overall influence. He distinguishes natural rapport with some students from actively rewarding likeability, and recommends sticking rigidly to the classroom management plan and using random methods, like pulling names from a hat, to eliminate any appearance of bias.
points: Recognize that favoritism is usually invisible to the teacher but obvious to students.
Apply the classroom management plan consistently to every student, regardless of likeability.
Give every student the same warmth and attention rather than reserving it for easier students.
Use random selection, like pulling names from a hat, for privileges and turns.
Don't let a student's difficult behavior earn them less kindness - that reinforces the behavior.
quotes: Favoritism is an insidious snake that wriggles unnoticed under your classroom door, poisoning morale from the inside out. Left unchecked, it will slither into every area of classroom management.
When you play favorites, you give rise to a class system—where certain students are socially grouped and labeled as special or entitled or somehow better than others.
If you play favorites—affording special privileges or attention for some and not others—every student will know it. And they’ll simmer with resentment because of it.
This is a highly manipulative and surprisingly common form of classroom management that reinforces outcast, rebel-like, and unruly behavior.
Playing favorites will undermine your efforts to increase your likeability , build rapport with students, and acquire behavior-changing leverage.
Follow your classroom management plan , regardless of who breaks your rules. Don’t yell, scold, berate, or take misbehavior personally.
